notes: Ruling slot 22 holds the Paraguayan Armed Forces (Stroessner is general and commander-in-chief); the Colorado Party, the regime's civilian pillar, is moved from MD slot 14 (no starting popularity) to coalition slot 13. PLR in 2 (MD successor PLRA), Levi Ruffinelli's legal Liberal Party in 16. Creydt's expelled Maoist wing in 19, Soler's pro-Soviet PCP in 4. Islamic slots use small Lebanese/Syrian/Palestinian merchant milieus of Asunción and Encarnación.

0.name: La Técnica
0.text:
La Técnica is the surveillance and interrogation office of the Ministry of the Interior, set up in the mid-1950s with the help of American advisers and run by Antonio Campos Alum. From its offices in Asunción it keeps files on Liberals, Febreristas, communists and wavering Colorados, and it is the regime's most direct link to Washington's hemispheric security network.

Its creed is simple: communism is the enemy and the United States the indispensable ally. Its leverage lies in its archives, its training ties to American programmes and its quiet cooperation with Argentine and Brazilian services against Paraguayan exiles.

1.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Party grew out of a Christian democratic movement founded in 1960 by Catholic students and professionals around Luis Alfonso Resck. The regime refuses it legal recognition, so its activists work through parishes, the Catholic University and exile networks, while Resck is repeatedly jailed and expelled.

Inspired by Chilean and Venezuelan Christian democracy, it calls for free elections, agrarian reform and Catholic social teaching against both Stroessner's personal rule and Marxism. Western in outlook yet critical of American support for the dictatorship, its strength lies in the reforming wing of the Church and the youth it is radicalising.

2.name: Partido Liberal Radical
2.text:
The Radical Liberal Party is the larger heir of Paraguay's historic Liberal Party, organised in 1967 when most Liberals decided to contest Stroessner's managed elections. Its candidate Gustavo González took about a fifth of the official vote in 1968, and it now occupies most of the minority seats the electoral law reserves for the opposition.

It stands for constitutional government, civil liberties and an end to the permanent state of siege, drawing on the old Liberal heartlands and urban professionals. Pro-American and anti-communist, it hopes Washington will press for genuine elections, though its participation also lends the regime a democratic façade.

3.name: Partido Revolucionario Febrerista
3.text:
The Revolutionary Febrerista Party takes its name from the February Revolution of 1936 that brought Colonel Rafael Franco to power. Legalised again in 1964 after long years of exile, it ran Carlos Caballero Gatti for president in 1968 and survives as a small, tolerated opposition party.

Febrerismo blends nationalism with democratic socialism: land reform, labour rights, a strong economic role for the state and solidarity with the democratic left of Latin America. Its base lies among teachers, students and urban professionals, and its leverage comes from ties to the Socialist International and to the large exile communities in Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

4.name: Partido Comunista Paraguayo
4.text:
The Paraguayan Communist Party has been outlawed for most of its existence and is hunted relentlessly by the police. After the destruction of its guerrilla front FULNA and a bitter split, the pro-Soviet majority expelled its veteran leader Óscar Creydt and now follows general secretary Miguel Ángel Soler, with much of its cadre in exile.

It seeks a broad anti-dictatorial front leading to a people's democracy, follows Moscow's line closely and now rejects guerrilla adventures. Its leverage is modest: clandestine cells among workers, students and peasants, a press smuggled in from Buenos Aires, and the backing of the Soviet-aligned parties of the hemisphere.

5.name: Generación del 14 de Mayo
5.text:
The Generation of 14 May gathers veterans and heirs of the 1959 Movimiento 14 de Mayo and of the guerrilla columns crushed in the early 1960s. Scattered between student rooms in Asunción and exile flats in Buenos Aires and Posadas, they argue over Cuba, Che Guevara's death in Bolivia and the lessons of their own defeats.

They reject both the cautious legal opposition and Moscow's line, insisting that only armed struggle can bring down a regime that fixes every election. Their numbers are tiny, but they draw on radical students, disillusioned young Liberals and Febreristas and the networks of the exile community.

6.name: Ñande Retã
6.text:
Ñande Retã is the hard nationalist milieu of historians, Chaco War veterans and Guaraní-language writers who carry on the revisionism of the late Juan E. O'Leary. They venerate Francisco Solano López, regard the War of the Triple Alliance as a crime of foreign capital, and dominate commemorations, school textbooks and the patriotic press.

They distrust Brazilian expansion along the Paraná, resent American cultural influence and want an autarkic, corporatist and Guaraní-speaking nation closed to cosmopolitan liberalism. Their leverage is ideological: the regime borrows their rhetoric, and many officers and Colorado cadres share their instincts.

7.name: Departamento de Investigaciones de la Policía de la Capital
7.native_full: Departamento de Investigaciones de la Policía de la Capital
7.text:
The Department of Investigations of the Asunción police is the political police of the regime, directed by Pastor Coronel. Its cells hold communists, peasant organisers and opposition students without trial, and its informers reach into every neighbourhood, market and university faculty.

It answers only to Stroessner and the Interior Ministry, treats foreign criticism of human rights abuses with contempt and is wary even of American diplomats who ask questions. Its leverage is fear: control of arrests, torture and exile, as well as a share in the protection rackets of the border trade, makes it a power bloc in its own right.

8.name: Ahl Jabal Amil
8.text:
The People of Jabal Amil are the few Lebanese Shia families who trade in Encarnación and Asunción, sending remittances home to the villages of southern Lebanon. They meet in private homes for Ashura and the major feasts, as no mosque yet exists in the country.

They look with pride to Imam Musa al-Sadr, elected in 1969 to lead the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon, and favour his message of dignity for the dispossessed through peaceful organisation. Loyal to Paraguay and its government, their influence rests only on commerce and family networks.

9.name: Halqat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Asunción who pass around sermons and pamphlets from the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini teaches. They are pious, intense and almost invisible to Paraguayan society.

They believe Muslims should be ruled by the learned clergy rather than by kings or secular parties, and they despise both American power and godless communism. In Paraguay they have no political weight at all; their importance lies in the contacts they keep with radical clerical networks in Lebanon and Iraq.

10.name: Musalla de Asunción
10.text:
The Asunción Prayer Room is the modest gathering place of Sunni merchants of Syrian, Lebanese and Palestinian origin, many of them textile and hardware traders in the capital's commercial streets. Older members keep the faith quietly while their children grow up speaking Spanish and Guaraní.

Respectful of authority, they avoid politics, maintain good relations with the Colorado establishment and receive Qur'ans and literature through the Muslim World League in Mecca. Their outlook is conservative, pious and loyal to the Gulf monarchies, and their small influence comes from commercial wealth and charitable giving.

11.name: Halqat al-Umma
11.text:
The Umma Circle is a tiny group of Palestinian-born students and shop assistants in Asunción, shaken by the defeat of 1967 and drawn to pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir that reach them from Jordan and Lebanon. They meet discreetly and attract the occasional curiosity of the police.

They reject nationalism, Arab socialism and the Western order alike, calling for a restored caliphate that would unite all Muslims and liberate Palestine. In Paraguay they are politically negligible, and their only leverage is the anger of a displaced generation and its ties to the wider diaspora.

12.name: Ikhwan al-Parana
12.text:
The Brothers of the Paraná are a study circle of young men of Syrian and Lebanese descent in Encarnación who read the works of Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in Spanish and Arabic editions. They organise Qur'an lessons, charity for newcomers and Arabic classes for children.

They want Muslims to rediscover Islam as a complete way of life through education, charity and moral reform rather than violence. They avoid Paraguayan politics entirely, and their modest leverage lies in community welfare and links to Brotherhood sympathisers in Argentina and Brazil.

13.name: Asociación Nacional Republicana – Partido Colorado
13.text:
The Colorado Party is the regime's mass organisation and one pillar of Stroessner's 'granite unity' of government, armed forces and party. Purged of dissidents since 1959, it is chaired by Juan Ramón Chaves, while Stroessner is its candidate and undisputed leader; membership is all but obligatory for civil servants, officers and teachers.

Through its local seccionales it hands out jobs, land titles and favours down to the smallest village, mobilises crowds and watches the neighbourhoods. Fiercely anti-communist and pro-American, its leverage is patronage: whoever controls the party machine controls access to the state.

14.name: Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya
14.text:
The Paraguayan Episcopal Conference speaks for the Catholic hierarchy, the only institution the regime cannot simply dissolve. Since Vatican II and the Medellín conference of 1968 the bishops have grown openly critical, and clashes multiplied in 1969 over police raids, the expulsion of Jesuit priests and attacks on the Christian Agrarian Leagues. Bishop Ramón Bogarín Argaña is among its most outspoken voices.

It demands respect for human rights, an end to torture and land for the peasantry, while remaining socially conservative and anti-communist. Its leverage is moral authority over an overwhelmingly Catholic population and a network of parishes, schools and the Catholic University.

15.name: Asociación Rural del Paraguay
15.text:
The Rural Association of Paraguay, founded in 1885, represents the cattle ranchers who own much of the Chaco and the eastern grasslands. Its annual exhibition in Mariano Roque Alonso is a showcase where ministers, generals and estancieros meet, and many of its members hold Colorado posts or military rank.

It wants secure property, cheap credit, low export taxes on beef and an end to any talk of land reform. It supports the regime as a guarantor of order and of good relations with Washington, and its leverage lies in land, export earnings and close personal ties to the officer corps.

16.name: Partido Liberal
16.text:
The Liberal Party is the smaller Liberal wing led by Carlos Levi Ruffinelli, which accepted legal status from the regime in the early 1960s and was denounced by other Liberals as collaborationist. Levi Ruffinelli polled only a few per cent in the 1968 presidential election, yet the party keeps a foothold in Congress.

It defends the nineteenth-century liberal creed of free enterprise, private property, open trade and limited government, and is firmly pro-American. Its base is a circle of Asunción lawyers, merchants and old Liberal families, and its leverage lies in its legal status and its value to the regime as a tame opposition.

17.name: Asociación Indigenista del Paraguay
17.text:
The Paraguayan Indigenist Association, founded in 1942, brings together anthropologists, missionaries and educated Paraguayans concerned with the country's indigenous peoples, drawing on the work of ethnographers such as León Cadogan. It documents the Guaraní and Chaco peoples and protests as ranchers and colonists advance into the eastern forests.

It calls for secure land for indigenous communities, protection of the Atlantic forest and the Chaco wilderness, and respect for native cultures and languages. Small and scholarly, it has no mass base, but it carries weight with the Church and with foreign academics and institutions.

18.name: Ligas Agrarias Cristianas
18.text:
The Christian Agrarian Leagues are a peasant movement born in the early 1960s from Catholic Action and rural parishes in Misiones, Paraguarí, Caaguazú and San Pedro. Thousands of smallholders have joined them, organising cooperatives, communal farms and their own schools, and they are already the target of police harassment.

They reject both Colorado clientelism and the latifundio, calling for land to those who work it, communal production and a society built on Christian solidarity rather than profit. Wary of both blocs, their leverage lies in rural mobilisation and the protection of sympathetic priests and bishops.

19.name: Los creydistas
19.text:
The creydistas are the followers of Óscar Creydt, the veteran communist leader expelled from the Paraguayan Communist Party in 1967 after the split over the failed guerrilla war and the Sino-Soviet dispute. They maintain their own party apparatus in exile and claim to be the true Communist Party.

They denounce Moscow as revisionist, praise Mao Zedong's China and call for a prolonged people's war based on the peasantry. Small and isolated, they compete bitterly with the pro-Soviet communists for a few dozen cadres among exiles, students and rural militants.

20.name: Movimiento Popular Colorado
20.text:
The Colorado Popular Movement was founded in 1959 by Colorado dissidents driven into exile after Stroessner purged the party. Its best-known figure is Epifanio Méndez Fleitas, the former central bank chief whose populist following once rivalled Stroessner's own, and it operates mainly from Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

It claims to be the authentic, popular Colorado Party, promising democracy, social justice for peasants and workers and an end to military tutelage. Nationalist and anti-communist but hostile to the dictatorship, its leverage lies in its appeal to rank-and-file Colorados and to the hundreds of thousands of Paraguayans living in Argentina.

21.name: Guión Rojo
21.text:
Guión Rojo is the hardline cadre of Colorado enforcers who keep alive the spirit of the shock troops of the 1940s and of the py nandí militias of the 1947 civil war. They run the toughest seccionales, break up opposition rallies with clubs and see themselves as the party's guard against Liberals and communists.

They stand for a militarised, one-party nation, the cult of order and loyalty to the leader, and despise elections and parliamentary compromise. Their leverage lies in street violence, their links to the police and the regime's need for loyal muscle in every district.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de la Nación
22.text:
The Paraguayan Armed Forces are the backbone of the regime of General Alfredo Stroessner, who seized power in 1954 and remains commander-in-chief while serving as president. The state of siege is renewed every ninety days, and key units such as the First Cavalry Division under General Andrés Rodríguez guard the capital.

The officer corps is bound to Stroessner and the Colorado Party by promotions, land grants and business opportunities. Staunchly anti-communist and a reliable partner of the United States, which supplies training and equipment, the military holds the decisive leverage of force and the final word on every succession.

23.name: La Casa López
23.text:
The House of López is the romantic cult around the family of Carlos Antonio López and his son Marshal Francisco Solano López, who ruled Paraguay as a hereditary dynasty until 1870. Descendants of the Marshal and Eliza Lynch are honoured guests at patriotic ceremonies, and the Marshal's remains rest in the National Pantheon of Heroes.

Its admirers dream of a paternal, hereditary authority above the parties, an independent nation strong enough to defy its giant neighbours. The idea has no organised following, but its symbolism pervades official nationalism and the regime takes care to claim the López legacy for itself.
